title: Your Students Are on Their Best Behavior. Don't Waste It.
author: Debbie
summary: Writing under the pen name Debbie for the Shift Happens newsletter, a 35-plus-year teaching veteran unpacks the classroom "honeymoon period" and argues teachers waste it by focusing on rule enforcement rather than value-modeling. She traces how the early-year compliance students show dissolves once academic struggle, embarrassment, or a sense of failure triggers a threat response in the brain, which then undercuts the very trust required for learning. Her core claim is that the first weeks of school should not be spent extending compliance through rule reminders, but designing experiences that let students practice the behaviors teachers actually want to see. She grounds this in the research link between students' sense of belonging, teacher relationships, and academic engagement, framing safety and trust as prerequisites for cognition rather than soft extras. Two concrete opening-week activities anchor the piece: a small-group T-chart distinguishing threatening from safe classroom behaviors, and a trust-building blindfolded-navigation game using only verbal guidance. The piece closes by reframing the goal of the first weeks as immersion in lived experience of expectations, not verbal warnings about them.
points: Reframes the classroom honeymoon period as a narrow window for modeling values through experience, not for issuing rule reminders that quietly erode once academic threat appears.
Links the neuroscience of threat detection directly to instructional design: a student's brain that senses embarrassment or failure activates defenses that block the pathways needed for learning.
Recommends replacing prohibitive language ("don't shout out," "be respectful") with structured practice activities that let students experience the target behavior directly.

Offers two field-tested first-week activities — a safe/unsafe behavior T-chart and a trust-building blind-guidance game — as concrete vehicles for establishing classroom safety before academic demands intensify.
Positions safety and trust as the foundation underneath all other classroom management, arguing that firm expectations and safety-building are complementary, not opposing, goals.
quotes: Once a student's brain senses threat, that early willingness to go along begins to dissolve. An I'll get you before you get me kind of defense can start to take over.

Those small interactions help shape how students feel about you and your classroom. And that matters. Decades of research have linked students' sense of belonging and their relationships with teachers to engagement and academic success.

That matters because when the brain senses a threat, it puts up roadblocks and interferes with the pathways we need for learning. Building trust and respect can help keep those defenses from going up.

Pair students and have one walk backward across the room while their partner guides them using only weird sound effects and one-word commands such as "Left!" "Right!" or "Stop!" Let two groups go at a time.
Students are learning what your classroom is like from what happens in it, not from what you tell them it's going to be like.
Set up as many opportunities for success as possible so your students can be directly immersed in what the expectations look like, feel like, and sound like.
